title: Physiography of India
summary: The Indian mainland extends from 8°4′N to 37°6′N latitude and from 68°7′E to 97°25′E longitude; its north–south extent is 3,214 km and east–west extent 2,933 km. India covers 3.28 million sq km — about 2.4% of the world's land area — and is the seventh largest country. The Tropic of Cancer (23°30′N) passes through the middle and divides it into two almost equal parts. The 82°30′E longitude, passing through Mirzapur (UP), is the Standard Meridian; it was chosen because there is a time lag of almost two hours between Gujarat and Arunachal Pradesh. India has 15,200 km of land boundary and a 6,100 km coastline.

India lies wholly in the northern and eastern hemispheres. It is bounded by the Arabian Sea (west), Bay of Bengal (east) and Indian Ocean (south). Pakistan and Afghanistan lie to the north-west; China (Tibet), Nepal and Bhutan to the north; Bangladesh and Myanmar to the east; Sri Lanka (across the Palk Strait) and the Maldives to the south. Indira Point (6°45′N, Nicobar) is the southernmost point of India and Kanyakumari (8°4′N) of the mainland.

Locational significance: India is the largest country of South Asia and lies at the centre of the Indian Ocean, commanding sea routes between Europe, Africa, South-East and East Asia and Oceania — so it has had trade relations across the sea since ancient times. Mountain passes such as Nathu La (Sikkim), Shipki La (Himachal), Zoji La and Burzil (J&K) and Jelep La (Kalimpong–Lhasa route) carried trade, travellers, ideas and culture.

1. The Northern Mountains — (i) the Himalayas: young fold mountains, the highest in the world, a natural barrier running about 2,500 km from the Indus to the Brahmaputra; width 400 km in the west to 150 km in the east. Three parallel ranges: Greater Himalaya or Himadri (average 6,000 m; snow-bound, most continuous; peaks Mt. Everest 8,848 m — highest in the world, Kanchenjunga — highest in India, Makalu, Dhaulagiri, Nanga Parbat; passes Bara Lacha La, Shipki La, Nathu La, Zoji La, Bomdi La; source of the Ganga and Yamuna); Lesser Himalaya or Himachal (1,000–4,500 m; Pir Panjal, Dhaula Dhar and Mahabharat ranges; hill stations Shimla, Mussoorie, Nainital, Darjeeling; Kashmir, Kullu and Kangra valleys); Outer Himalaya or Shiwaliks (900–1,100 m, the outermost; 'duns' like Dehra Dun lie between the Shiwaliks and Himachal). (ii) Trans-Himalaya: from north to south the Karakoram (K2, second highest peak in the world), Ladakh and Zaskar ranges; the Indus flows between the Zaskar and Ladakh ranges. (iii) Purvanchal hills: Mishmi, Patkai, Naga and Mizo hills, and the Meghalaya plateau with the Garo, Khasi and Jaintia hills.

2. The Northern Plains — formed by alluvium of the Indus, Ganga and Brahmaputra; about 2,400 km long, 300 km wide in the west to 150 km in the east; covers Punjab, Haryana, UP, Bihar, West Bengal and Assam. One of the most fertile plains in the world (wheat, rice, sugarcane, pulses, oilseeds, jute). Two parts: the Western (Punjab) plain, made by the Satluj, Beas and Ravi, with doabs; and the Ganga–Brahmaputra plain. Khadar is new alluvium flooded every year; bhangar is old alluvium never flooded.

3. The Peninsular Plateau — a triangular tableland of ancient Gondwana rocks, about 5 lakh sq km. The Narmada divides it into: (i) the Central Highlands — the Aravalli (highest peak Gurushikhar, 1,722 m, near Mt. Abu), the Malwa plateau (Betwa, Chambal, Ken rivers) and the Chhota Nagpur plateau; the Narmada flows west in a rift valley between the Vindhya and Satpura ranges; (ii) the Deccan Plateau — its black-soil area of volcanic origin, the 'Deccan Trap', is good for cotton and sugarcane. The Western Ghats (Sahyadri) are continuous, average 1,000 m, run 1,600 km along the west coast; highest peak Anaimudi (2,695 m), also Doda Betta and Makurti; passes Pal Ghat, Thal Ghat, Bhor Ghat; Jog Falls on the Sharavati. The Eastern Ghats are discontinuous and lower (average 600 m), from south of the Mahanadi to the Nilgiris; highest peak Mahendragiri (1,501 m); cut by the Mahanadi, Godavari, Krishna and Kaveri. The Nilgiri hills join the two Ghats.

4. The Indian (Thar) Desert — west of the Aravallis in Rajasthan and Gujarat; less than 150 mm rain (the monsoon winds blow parallel to the Aravallis); thorny bushes, sand dunes; the Luni is the main river.

5. The Coastal Plains — the western coastal plain is narrow (10–20 km) from the Rann of Kachchh to Kanyakumari, with the Konkan, Karnataka and Malabar coasts (Vembanad is a famous lagoon on the Malabar coast). The eastern coastal plain is wider (about 120 km) — Northern Circars and Coromandel Coast — with deltas of the Mahanadi, Godavari, Krishna and Kaveri; Chilka, the largest salt-water lake, lies south of the Mahanadi delta. They grow rice, coconut and spices and have fishing, trade and ports.
6. The Islands — Andaman and Nicobar (204 islands in the Bay of Bengal; active volcano on Barren Island) and Lakshadweep (43 coral islands in the Arabian Sea; capital Kavaratti).

A drainage system is the flow of surface water mainly through rivers; the area drained by a river and its tributaries is a drainage basin. Himalayan rivers — Indus (Jhelum, Chenab, Ravi, Beas, Satluj), Ganga (Yamuna, Ramganga, Ghaghara, Gomti, Gandak, Kosi) and Brahmaputra (Dibang, Lohit, Tista) — are perennial (fed by glaciers and rain), erode deep valleys, have meandering courses and are good for irrigation in the plains. Peninsular rivers — Mahanadi, Godavari (longest in the peninsula), Krishna and Kaveri flow east into the Bay of Bengal; only the Narmada and Tapi flow west into the Arabian Sea through rift valleys and form estuaries. They are seasonal (rain-fed), form waterfalls and rapids and are good for hydro-power. Cities grow on rivers: Delhi (Yamuna), Patna (Ganga), Guwahati (Brahmaputra), Nashik (Godavari), Cuttack (Mahanadi).

Less than 1% of the world's water is usable fresh water. Sewage causes about 70% of river pollution. The government runs the Ganga Action Plan and the National River Conservation Plan; water harvesting retains monsoon water in river basins, and civic organisations and people's movements spread awareness about polluted rivers.

vsa: Passes are natural gaps through mountain ranges. Passes like Nathu La, Shipki La, Zoji La and Jelep La provided routes for trade, travellers and the exchange of ideas and culture between India and Tibet/Central Asia, and they are also strategically important.

or: Why does India have good trade relations with many countries across the sea?

India lies at the centre of the Indian Ocean, surrounded by sea on three sides, and commands the sea routes between Europe and Africa on one side and South-East Asia, East Asia and Oceania on the other. So it has traded with many countries since ancient times.

vsa: Find the minimum number of states you need to cross if you travel from Gujarat to Assam by road.

Gujarat → Madhya Pradesh (or Rajasthan) → Uttar Pradesh → Bihar → West Bengal → Assam. You must cross at least four states (e.g. Madhya Pradesh/Rajasthan, Uttar Pradesh, Bihar and West Bengal) before entering Assam.
Mention any two features of the Western Ghats.

(1) They run continuously for about 1,600 km parallel to the west coast with an average height of 1,000 m, and can be crossed only through passes like Pal Ghat, Thal Ghat and Bhor Ghat. (2) Their highest peak is Anaimudi (2,695 m); rivers flowing west form rapids and waterfalls such as Jog Falls.
Explain any two characteristics of the Northern Plains of India.

(1) They are formed by alluvial deposits of the Indus, Ganga and Brahmaputra and are among the most fertile plains in the world. (2) They are about 2,400 km long and level, with good irrigation, so wheat, rice, sugarcane and jute are grown; they are densely populated.
Name two Purvanchal hills and mention the countries in which the Greater Himalaya is situated.
Purvanchal hills: Patkai and Mizo (also Mishmi, Naga). The Greater Himalaya lies in India, Nepal and Bhutan.
What is a pass? Name any two passes situated in the Greater Himalaya.
A pass is a natural gap or route through a range of mountains or hills. Passes in the Greater Himalaya: Shipki La, Nathu La (also Zoji La, Bara Lacha La, Bomdi La).
sa: Explain any three differences between the Himalayan and the Peninsular drainage systems.

(1) Himalayan rivers are perennial, fed by glaciers and rain; Peninsular rivers are seasonal and rain-fed. (2) Himalayan rivers erode deep valleys and have long, meandering courses that shift; Peninsular rivers flow in shallow, fixed valleys and form waterfalls and rapids. (3) Himalayan rivers flow through fertile plains and are ideal for irrigation and navigation; Peninsular rivers are better for hydro-power. (Most Peninsular rivers flow east to the Bay of Bengal; only the Narmada and Tapi flow west.)

or: Explain any three main characteristics of the Western Ghats.

(1) They lie along the western edge of the Deccan plateau and run parallel to the west coast for about 1,600 km. (2) They are continuous and higher than the Eastern Ghats (average 1,000 m); Anaimudi (2,695 m) is the highest peak, with Doda Betta and Makurti. (3) They can be crossed only through passes (Pal, Thal, Bhor Ghat); the Godavari, Bhima and Krishna rise here and flow east, while short west-flowing streams form waterfalls like Jog Falls.

sa: Explain any three features of the Central Highlands of India.

(1) They lie north of the Narmada, between the river and the Northern Plains. (2) They include the Aravalli range (highest peak Gurushikhar near Mt. Abu), the Malwa plateau (drained by the Betwa, Chambal and Ken) and the Chhota Nagpur plateau (Mahadeo, Kaimur and Maikal hills). (3) The Narmada flows west in a rift valley between the Vindhya and Satpura ranges.
'India has a unique geographical location.' Support the statement.

(1) It lies in the northern and eastern hemispheres between 8°4′N–37°6′N and 68°7′E–97°25′E, with the Tropic of Cancer passing through the middle. (2) It is surrounded by sea on three sides and lies at the centre of the Indian Ocean, commanding sea routes between Europe/Africa and East Asia, which helps trade. (3) The Himalayas form a natural barrier in the north, while passes link it with neighbours for trade and cultural exchange.
Explain the main features of the Himadri (Greater Himalaya) range.

(1) It is the northernmost and most continuous range, with an average height of 6,000 m and width of 120–190 km. (2) It is snow-bound and many glaciers descend from it; the Ganga and Yamuna originate here. (3) It has the highest peaks — Mt. Everest (8,848 m), Kanchenjunga, Makalu, Dhaulagiri, Nanga Parbat — and high passes like Shipki La, Nathu La and Zoji La.
What are the two divisions of the Northern Plains of India? Write two features of each.

(1) The Western Plain: formed by the Indus system rivers (Satluj, Beas, Ravi), lies west of the Aravallis, and has doabs — fertile land between two rivers. (2) The Ganga–Brahmaputra Plain: formed by the Ganga and Brahmaputra, very fertile and densely populated; early civilisations grew in such river valleys because of fertile land and water.
Why are rivers important for life? Explain.

(1) They supply fresh water for drinking, irrigation and industries and maintain the water table. (2) They carry fertile sediments, remove excess water and are used for navigation, hydro-power and tourism (boating, rafting). (3) Many cities and holy places grew on their banks — Delhi on the Yamuna, Patna on the Ganga, Guwahati on the Brahmaputra — so they are called lifelines.

la: Explain India's geographical location with reference to its surrounding water bodies, neighbouring countries and southernmost points.

(1) The mainland extends from 8°4′N to 37°6′N and 68°7′E to 97°25′E; the Tropic of Cancer divides it into two halves and 82°30′E is the Standard Meridian. (2) Water bodies: the Arabian Sea in the west, the Bay of Bengal in the east and the Indian Ocean in the south. (3) Neighbours: Pakistan and Afghanistan (north-west); China, Nepal and Bhutan (north); Bangladesh and Myanmar (east); Sri Lanka across the Palk Strait and the Maldives (south). (4) Southernmost points: Kanyakumari (8°4′N) on the mainland and Indira Point (Nicobar Islands) for the whole country. (5) Its central position in the Indian Ocean gives it command over sea routes. (6) The Himalayas protect it in the north while passes connect it with neighbours.
Describe the six physical divisions of India.

(1) Northern Mountains — Himalayas (Himadri, Himachal, Shiwaliks), Trans-Himalaya (Karakoram, Ladakh, Zaskar) and Purvanchal hills. (2) Northern Plains — fertile alluvial plains of the Indus, Ganga and Brahmaputra from Punjab to Assam. (3) Peninsular Plateau — triangular, ancient; Central Highlands and Deccan Plateau, with the Western and Eastern Ghats. (4) Indian (Thar) Desert — west of the Aravallis, under 150 mm rain, sand dunes. (5) Coastal Plains — narrow western (Konkan, Karnataka, Malabar) and wider eastern (Northern Circars, Coromandel) with deltas. (6) Islands — Andaman & Nicobar in the Bay of Bengal and coral Lakshadweep in the Arabian Sea.
